Sydney, Dec., 19, 1963
Dear I and P.
We had quite a typical French departure from Noumea. The TAI large bus called
for ue at les Bungalows promptly at 2:30 in the afternon add then made other stops
on the road into town. The Prench and Australians piling on at each stop with
bundles, be bied, basicets and blankets in a velter of confusion.
Eventually we
arrived at the TAI city office where there ensued a long unexplained delay. Pinally
in official announced in rapid fire French and then in halting English that the air-
plane was having mechanical trouble and we would wait there to see whether or not
we'd fly.
After an hour more all the French began scrambling back on the bus and
, someone said " We're Going". The drive to the airport, 30 miles, was magnificent.
When we got there all was confusion compounded. There must have been 300 people in
and around the small station with baggage scattered all over the place. It reminded
me of the time Bondy and I left Nanicing for Hankow during the war.
We took an over
crowded lighter out to the steamer in mid river.
You cannot possibly conceive of
such confusion. Each coolie trying to out screech
the others. Bondy reassured one
American inexperienced traveler who had 17 different pieces of baggage that out of
that bedlam would come order and he'd find all 17 pieces in his stateroom. It
seemed like a thousand to one shot but that is just what happened to our friend and
also to us. So it was with the French in Tantouta airport at Noumea. Eventually
it all straightened out, we got on the airplane, a Douglas DC & Jet; and we hsd a,
very comfortable flight to Sydney. However,
I am glad to be away from the French.
The PAA #1 in Australia, Rush Clark, met us at the airport, whisiced us through
customs, and drove us into the new Menzirs Hotel, after going by his offioe to pick
up our mail. Debby and I had a late snack and read our mail, a real treat.
The next
day, Wed. the 18th, I had lunch at the American Club with Rush Clark and Debby
lunched with his wife. Then that evening we all had drinks at Sir Hudson and Lady
Fysh's apartment after which they gave us a super dinner at a restaurant on Rose Bay
where the old flying boats used to base. Hudson Fysh ie an old World War I pilot
who was born in Tasmania and came back bere after the war to start Quantas which has
grown to be one of the largest airlines in the world. He and I served together on
the Executive Committee of IATA. He is plenty sharp- as evidence - we used to agree
on almost every issue. He is a real friend.
Dec. 20. This afternoon we're off for Cairnes en route Thursday Island. Of
course everything here is baokwards - as we go north it gets hotter and we plan to
travel light leaving our suit cases here at the hotel. We go out on the Great
Barrier Reef from Cairnes to Green Island for Sat. and Sunday the 2lst and 22nd.
Then on the 23rd we fly from Cairnes to Thursday.
Doc. 23rd. It didn't work out that way. When we arrived at Cairnes it seemed
best to make some changes in our plans. It would have been fun to have our Christmas
on Thursday Island but on the other hand we did not want to become a burden to
•Debby's friend Reg scott.
So we phoned him on the day after our arrival here (Dec.21)
and cleared a program to fly up there on the 26th arriving about 4:30 in the after-
noon and come back here on the 27th. Meanwhile we learned two things. One, Green
Island wassfull up for the holidays and couldn't take us, and two, that 1% 1s a park
where it is against the law to do any shelling. So we stayed in the Great Northern
at Cairnes.
unday the 22nd we took a boat - with about 100 other passengers - out the 1
miles to Green Island on the Great Barrieß. Reef.
lt is a beautiful coral 18lan
of some 30 acres entirely surrounded by coral reefs. We took a glass bottomed boat
trip. Looked at the world famous under water museum and enjoyed ourselves - but no
Then today we got a drive U.R. self Holden (General Motors) and drove on
the wrong side of the road 50 miles up the coast to the small town of Port Douglas
where a shell merchant by the name of Tom Scullett has quite a collection. He had
been recommended by a collector on Fiji. Debby bought quite a few shells and
established a good contact for future acquisitions. While she was talking shelle I
of a "Pub". They told me that at one time there were 17 Pubs on the main street
where now there was only this one. In their minds it was clear that civic importance
was measured in terms of the number of pubs. All this talk about pubs reminds me of
ABISH

the tine I had the honor of being President of the S.P.C.A., an organization which had
little to do with kindness to animals, the initials stood for the Shanghai Pub
Crawlers Association.
It seems that in the old days produce of the interior of North
queensland moved over rough roads by bullook drawn carts which descended from the
"Pable Land" to the Port of Douglas.
Then came the rail road to Cairnes and that
was the end of Port Douglas. As you get around the world it is rather sad to see
how changes beyond the control of the individual erode values. I remember when Ed
Queeney of Monsanto Chemical said that one of the dad effects of chemical researon
was the damage done to some old established businesses such, for example, as the
leather trade or sponge divers.
This reaction la evident in the local economy
where the formerly important pearl button industry has been almost wholly supplanted
by plastios. As a result the Queensland government had been experimenting with the
culture of artificial pearls. They have haddquite a bit of help from the Japanese
in return for which technical assistance the Japs take over the marketing of the
pearls, at which, they are most experienced and I suspect reap the largest share of
One of the fringe benefits of our travels in the tropics has been the Paw Paws
or Papayas. For 30 years I have tried in vain to like them but not until this trip
did I succeed. Also the Australian Mangos are as good as we have ever tasted.
Deo. 25th. This year Christmes for us 1e just the 25th of Beenher, but ve're
neither homesick or unhappy. Yesterday weihired a car and driver and motored up
to the Table Lands about 1200 feet higher than Cairnes which of course is a sea level
port and at sea level. We saw "the most beautiful rail road station in the world"
and by golly it lived up to its billing. The station itself was much like any other
American station with tracks on either side but the entire 150 - 200 foot length was
a mass of beautiful ferns, orchids, frangi pani, tree ferns, traveller's palms and
flowering shrubs in a profusion of colors. Our driver was an old soldier and had
done quite a bit of prospecting. He told us all about the old days before the rail
road, the bullook carts and the early pioneers of whom his father was one. We asked
him about the aborigines, whom he called "abos", who are much more in evidence in
this part of Australia than elsewbere.
I told him that Capt. Cook had to put in to
shore for pepairs to his ship just notth of here and was much surprised to find no
natives at all nor did any come around for the whole three months he was there. Our
driver eaid that was because the abos lived up on the Table land where they lead a
nomadic life following the game and fishing in the numerous streams, In faot he
said that one quite intelligent abo said to him " You know, sir, you white people
are making real progress - you do not work as hard as your father did and he in turn
did not work as hard as his father.
With us it is just the reverse. My grandfather
didn't do any work at all. He had a good life.
Then when the white man came my
father had to work, he couldn't just move around hunting and fishing. Then I came
along and I have to work much harder than my father did. We abos are sliding baok
as fast as you whites are going ahead."
1 Ded. 26ta, In route Cairns - Thursday Island.
We are flying in a twin engined
Pokker along the coast with the Great Barrier Reef clearly marked off to our right
about 15 miles.out from the coast. Cooktown, where Cook repaired his badly damaged
ship - is off to our right. Beyond lies the Coral Sea where some 200 miles out one
of the great naval engagements of World War II was fought. We were sort of hoping to
fly over to Papua and New Guinea. We had heard that up in the mountains at a place
called Goroke there would be a big gathering of tribesmen and a most interesting show.
we actually applied for a permit to fly to Port Moresby but we then learned that the
big pow pow of natives had been called off and that we might have alot of trouble
securing permits to go beyond Port Moresby because of trouble with Sukarno over the
border between Australia and Indonesia. While there may be no real trouble you can
sure get plenty of run around from the bureaucrats who control the granting of travel
So tonight we'll be with Debby's friend Reg Scott and tomorrow we'll fly as
far as Rockhampton. It would have been intensely interesting to see the areas in lew
Guinea where Bill Hawkins spent so much time during the war and perhaps get over to
Rabaul and the Solomon Islands where Bill Barrett operated his P.T. boat so effectively
but the will have to wait.

- 3-
Doc. 27th. En route south from Thursday Island. We arrived at Thured y which
is about twice as big as blay Island or actually two miles around. Debby's friend Reg
boott met us and escorted us to the Grand Hotel on a slight rise about the harbor.
ur room was on the second floor reached from an open porch.
It had a large door
opening on to the porch but no other ventilation whatever and it was hot. Thursday
Island is just a little more than 10 degrees below the equator. Reg told us that
the coldest day last winter the temperature dropped to 68 degrees at 2 A.M.
Grand boasts of "Septic accomodations" which means you con't have to use a
"Chic
dale". However, the toilet for men, such as it was, was at the end of the long
wooden porch and the ladies around the corner from there.
We left these sumptious
surroundings at once and went to keg's house by taxi. It is on a hill side over
looking the harbor. We met Mr.s Scott, very cordial and nice and their little girl
age 5, quite cute. Mrs. Scott busied herself with getting dinner while Debby and
Reg started looking over drawer after drawer of fine shells, many quite rare. He
let her buy anything she wanted except two or three he wanted to keep for one
reason or another.
Dinner was announced at 7 P.M. and we had perfectly delicious
apparently with a large deep freeze filled with venison, wild pig and mackerel the •
scott family pretty much lives off the tani, after dinner Reg andy Debby looked st
shells until 11 P.M., agreed on a selection, got together on cost and he agreed to
psor and ship to Captiva.
oR more hospitable. He walked down to the hotel with us and we said our au revoirs.
It was "Caberet" night at the Grand. Alot of pretty rough looking customers, black,
white and brown were dringing beer and dancing to the music of a three man orchestra
whose playing xxx made up in sound for what it lacked in quality. In our room on
the second floor balcony we haddall the privacy of the proverbial gold fish for we
couldn't close our door without suffocating. However, the music or should I say
noise, abated around midnight and we slept until called at 6 a.m. to catch the
plane on which I am writing now. So Thursday Island has come and gone. It was two xa
ye irs ago that Debby got a letter from Keg scott in which he said that he wanted
to sell his collection. I said "Why don't you buy it ?" and Deb said "I wouldn't
want to buy any part of it without seeing it" so I said "let's go look at it ". "We
can't do that" said Deb and I said "Why not?" And here we are, mission secomplished.
Debby has some wonderful and very rare shells to add to her collection and is
quite happy.
Coming south we landed at Weipa on the York Peninsula. It is the
center of an almost unlimited supply of bauxite, the ore used to produce aluminum.
Further down the coast there are large coal deposits. They hope to combine the two
to produce aluminum econnmically. Our next stop is Cooktown and then Cairns
where wo he ve a four hour stopover before taking a larger and faster Viscount
to Rockhampton.
I'll get this off from Cairns as it is already too long. We'll probably
stLy several days in the Rockhampton area going out to the Great Barrier Reef and
seeing a number of shell dealers who have been highly recommended.
Then to
Sydney and across Australia to Pérth. We haven't decided whether we'll go by air,
train or bus. The latter would give us the best look at the country but four days
of that travel might be a little rough for us old folks. Anyway, our addrees until
ny next letter will be care of PAA, 82 Blizabeth St., Sydney.
May '64 bring you more - of everything you want.
Harold
